posts.title: Speculative Decoding: Draft Fast, Verify Once
posts.subtitle: A small draft model guesses ahead; the big model checks the guesses in a single pass.
posts.summary: Speculative decoding uses a cheap draft model to propose several tokens ahead, then lets the full model verify all of them in one forward pass instead of one token at a time. It produces the exact same output distribution as normal decoding, just faster, with the biggest wins at low concurrency and the smallest at high batch sizes.

slides.title: One Token at a Time Is the Real Speed Limit
bullets: Autoregressive decoding generates exactly one token per full forward pass through the model
Speculative decoding breaks that rule without changing what the model outputs

slides.title: Decoding Is Memory-Bound, Not Compute-Bound
slides.body: Generating one token means streaming every weight of a multi-billion-parameter model through the GPU, then throwing almost all of that compute away because the batch of 'work' is just one new token.
bullets: The GPU spends most of its time moving weights from HBM, not computing on them
Compute utilization during single-token decode is often a small fraction of peak, because arithmetic intensity is low per token

slides.title: Draft Many, Verify in Parallel
bullets: A small, cheap draft model (or an early-exit head of the same model) proposes K tokens ahead autoregressively
The large target model then scores all K draft tokens in a single forward pass, the same cost as generating one token normally
Each draft token is accepted if it matches what the target model would have sampled; the run stops at the first mismatch, where the target model's own sample replaces it
This acceptance/rejection rule is what makes the final output distribution mathematically identical to plain sampling from the target model

slides.title: Walking Through One Round
slides.body: Prompt: 'The capital of France is'. Draft model proposes 5 tokens: ' Paris, located on the Seine'.
bullets: Target model verifies all 5 in one pass: accepts 'Paris, located on the' (4 tokens match what it would have sampled)
Token 5 ('Seine') doesn't match; the target model's own sampled token replaces it and the round ends there
Net result: 4 tokens produced for roughly the cost of 1 target-model forward pass, instead of 5 separate passes

slides.title: Standard vs. Speculative Decoding

rows: ~1 per batch of K draft tokens
A draft model or early-exit head to host and sync

slides.title: Tradeoffs and When Not to Use It
bullets: Benefit shrinks at high batch sizes: once the GPU is already compute-bound serving many concurrent requests, there's little idle compute left for verification to exploit
Needs a draft model that's well-matched to the target's domain; a draft trained mostly on prose will have low acceptance rate on code, eroding the speedup
Adds operational cost: a second model to load, keep in sync with the target's tokenizer and version, and serve alongside it
Not worth it for very short generations, where draft/verify overhead can exceed the savings

slides.title: The Core Idea to Keep
bullets: Speculative decoding trades idle GPU compute during memory-bound decode for fewer sequential steps
It's a free lunch on output quality — the math guarantees the same distribution as standard sampling
Where it pays off most: single-stream, latency-sensitive serving with a draft model that's cheap and well-aligned to the target

questions.prompt: Why is single-token autoregressive decoding slow on modern GPUs?
options: It's memory-bandwidth bound: the GPU spends most of its time streaming model weights for very little compute per token
The GPU runs out of compute (FLOPs) generating a single token
Tokenization itself is the bottleneck
It requires recompiling the model for every token
questions.explanation: Generating one token requires moving the entire model's weights through the GPU for a tiny amount of actual arithmetic, so decode is bound by memory bandwidth, not compute — which is exactly the slack speculative decoding exploits.

questions.prompt: Does speculative decoding change the probability distribution of the generated text compared to standard sampling?
options: No — the accept/reject rule is designed so the final samples are statistically identical to sampling directly from the target model
Yes — it always produces higher-quality text than standard decoding
Yes — it strictly produces the single most likely token at each step (greedy decoding)
No — it only works with greedy decoding, never sampling
questions.explanation: The verification step accepts or rejects each draft token based on the target model's own probabilities, and resamples on rejection, which keeps the output distribution mathematically equivalent to plain sampling from the target model.

questions.prompt: When does speculative decoding help the least?
options: At high concurrency / large batch sizes, where the GPU is already compute-bound serving many requests
On a single, latency-sensitive request with no other traffic
When the draft model closely matches the target model's domain
On very long generations
questions.explanation: Speculative decoding exploits otherwise-idle compute during memory-bound decoding. At high batch sizes the GPU is already busy with useful compute across many requests, so there's less slack left to turn into a speedup.

posts.title: Reranking: The Second Pass That Fixes Bad Retrieval
posts.subtitle: Vector search casts a wide, fast net; a cross-encoder reranker catches what actually matters.
posts.summary: Vector search is fast because it compares precomputed, independent embeddings, but that independence costs precision. Reranking fixes this by running a slower cross-encoder — one that reads the query and each candidate together — over only the retriever's top candidates, trading a little latency for much better final ordering.

slides.title: Fast Retrieval and Accurate Retrieval Are Different Jobs
bullets: Vector search over millions of documents has to be fast, so it approximates
Reranking is the second, slower pass that recovers the accuracy that approximation gave up

slides.title: Bi-Encoders Score Query and Document Separately
slides.body: A standard embedding model (bi-encoder) encodes the query and each document independently into fixed vectors, then compares them with cosine similarity or dot product.
bullets: That independence is what makes ANN search over an HNSW or IVF index fast — embeddings are precomputed once, offline
But it also means the model never sees the query and document together, so it can't model fine-grained token-level interactions
Result: documents that share surface-level topic or vocabulary can outrank the one that actually answers the question

slides.title: Cross-Encoders Read Query and Document Together
bullets: A cross-encoder concatenates the query and a single candidate document into one input and runs them jointly through a transformer
Self-attention lets every query token attend directly to every document token, so it can catch exact phrase matches and precise relevance cues a bi-encoder misses
Far more accurate, but it must run once per candidate — it cannot be precomputed or indexed, so it doesn't scale to a whole corpus

slides.title: The Two-Stage Pipeline
bullets: Stage 1 — Retrieve: embed the query, run ANN search over the full corpus (HNSW/IVF), pull back a wide top-N (commonly 50-100 candidates)
Stage 2 — Rerank: run the cross-encoder on just those N candidates, paired with the query, to get a precise relevance score
Take the reranked top-k (often 3-10) as the final context handed to the LLM

slides.title: A Query Where Retrieval Alone Fails
slides.body: Query: 'how to configure retry backoff in boto3'.
bullets: Vector search returns 50 candidates; a generic 'AWS SDK overview' page ranks #2 purely on broad topical and keyword overlap
The specific 'botocore retry configuration' page — the one with the actual answer — only ranks #11 by embedding similarity
The cross-encoder reads query and document together, recognizes the precise phrase match on 'retry' and 'backoff' in context, and promotes it to #1 in the final top-5

slides.title: Bi-Encoder vs. Cross-Encoder
Tradeoffs and When to Skip It
bullets: Every reranked candidate costs one more transformer forward pass, so it adds real latency on top of retrieval
Picking N matters: too small and the right document may never make it into the candidate set at all; too large and reranking latency climbs linearly
Under a tight latency budget (sub-100ms) with no slack, or when the retriever's top-k is already small and reliable, the extra pass may not be worth it
Reranking fixes ordering, not recall — pair it with hybrid (keyword + vector) retrieval when exact term matches matter, since a bi-encoder can still miss a candidate entirely

slides.title: The Core Idea to Keep
bullets: Retrieval optimizes for recall at scale; reranking optimizes for precision on a short list
A cross-encoder is slower but strictly more accurate because it reads query and document together instead of comparing precomputed vectors
Use it as a second stage over the retriever's top-N, not as a replacement for retrieval

questions.prompt: Why can a bi-encoder (standard embedding search) rank an irrelevant document above the correct one?
options: It encodes the query and each document independently, so it can't model fine-grained interactions between specific query and document tokens
It always ranks documents randomly
It can only handle exact keyword matches, never semantic similarity
It reruns the full corpus through a transformer for every query, which introduces noise
questions.explanation: Because the bi-encoder compares precomputed, independently-encoded vectors, it loses the fine-grained token-level interaction a joint read of query and document would catch — which is exactly the gap a cross-encoder reranker closes.

questions.prompt: What does a cross-encoder reranker take as input?
options: The query and a single candidate document, concatenated and processed together in one forward pass
Only the precomputed document embeddings from the vector index
The entire corpus at once, scored in a single batch
Just the query, with no document at all
questions.explanation: A cross-encoder reads the query and one candidate together so self-attention can directly compare their tokens — that joint read is what a bi-encoder's separate encoding can't do, and why cross-encoders can't be precomputed or indexed.

questions.prompt: When is adding a reranking stage least worth it?
options: Under a very tight, sub-100ms latency budget with no slack for an extra forward pass per candidate
When the initial retrieval set is large and noisy
When precision on the final top-k matters a lot
When the corpus is large enough that recall is a concern
questions.explanation: Reranking adds one transformer forward pass per candidate on top of retrieval latency. When there's no latency budget left to spend, that cost can outweigh the precision gain, even though it would help in most other cases.

posts.title: Continuous Batching: No Idle GPUs Between Requests
posts.subtitle: Stop waiting for the slowest request in the batch to finish.
posts.summary: Static, request-level batching ties a whole batch's lifetime to its slowest member, wasting GPU cycles padding sequences that already finished. Continuous batching schedules at the granularity of a single decoding step instead: finished sequences are evicted immediately and new requests fill their slot on the very next forward pass, keeping GPU utilization high regardless of how unevenly requests finish.

slides.title: Why Your GPU Sits Idle Between Requests
slides.body: Continuous batching rewrites the LLM serving loop around one idea: don't wait for the slowest request in a batch before starting the next one.
bullets: Static batching: one slow request blocks the whole batch from being refreshed
Continuous batching: swap requests in and out at every decoding step
Reported gain: up to 36.9x higher throughput at equal latency (Orca, OSDI 2022)

slides.title: Static Batching Makes Fast Requests Wait for Slow Ones
slides.body: The obvious way to batch LLM requests — group N of them, run until every sequence finishes, then start the next batch — wastes most of the GPU's time in practice.
bullets: Requests in a batch rarely finish together: a 20-token reply and a 500-token reply get grouped, but the batch can't return until the 500-token one is done.
Once a short sequence finishes, its slot just pads with throwaway computation — real GPU cycles spent producing nothing usable.
New requests sit in the queue the entire time, even with spare capacity, because the scheduler only admits work at batch boundaries.

slides.title: Schedule at the Granularity of One Decoding Step
slides.body: Continuous batching — Orca's 'iteration-level scheduling' — treats every single forward pass, not every whole request, as the unit the scheduler controls.
bullets: After each decoding step, any sequence that just emitted an end token is evicted from the batch immediately — no waiting for stragglers.
The freed slot goes straight to a new request pulled from the queue, which joins the very next forward pass.
Batch membership can be completely different step to step — it's never 'closed' the way a static batch is.

slides.title: Selective Batching Makes Mixed-Length Batches Work
slides.body: Batching requests with different lengths and different amounts already generated isn't trivial — Orca solves it with 'selective batching.'
bullets: Rather than batching a whole Transformer layer naively, selective batching batches only the operations that tolerate different-length inputs (like the linear layers) and handles attention per request.
This is why continuous batching is almost always paired with a paged, non-contiguous KV cache: sequences enter and leave at arbitrary steps, so the cache can't assume one fixed block per batch.
The scheduler also enforces a memory budget per step — it won't admit a new request if there isn't enough free KV-cache space to hold it.

slides.title: Static vs. Continuous Batching
slides.body: The difference comes down to when the scheduler is allowed to change who's in the batch.

rows: Only at the next batch boundary
On the very next decoding step
Padded until the whole batch finishes
Drops as short sequences finish early
Stays high — slots are always refilled

slides.title: Four Requests, One Changing Batch
slides.body: A batch slot of size 4 serves requests A (10-token reply), B (200 tokens), C (15 tokens), and D (80 tokens), all arriving close together.
bullets: Step 10: A finishes and is evicted immediately; its slot goes to new request E from the queue — B, C, D keep generating uninterrupted.
Step 15: C finishes next; its slot goes to F. The batch is now B, D, E, F — a completely different lineup than at step 1.
Under static batching, none of this happens until B (the longest) finishes at step 200 — E and F would have sat in the queue the entire time.

slides.title: The Catch: Fairness and Scheduling Overhead
slides.body: Continuous batching maximizes throughput, but it introduces tradeoffs a scheduler has to actively manage.
bullets: A newly admitted request can be starved if the scheduler always prioritizes draining long-running sequences over admitting new ones — real schedulers cap how many new requests join per step to bound this.
Per-step scheduling overhead is real: deciding what to admit or evict every single iteration costs CPU time a simpler static-batch loop never pays.
It needs a KV-cache allocator built for dynamic add/remove (paged, not one contiguous block) — bolting continuous batching onto a naive fixed-size cache mostly doesn't work.
Skip it for: offline batch jobs where every request is known upfront and latency doesn't matter — static batching with a well-chosen batch size is simpler and just as efficient there.

slides.title: Keep the Batch Always Full
bullets: Static batching wastes GPU cycles padding finished sequences until the slowest request in the batch is done.
Continuous batching evicts and admits requests every decoding step, keeping GPU utilization high regardless of how unevenly requests finish.
It depends on a paged KV cache that can grow and shrink per sequence without big reshuffles.
It's the default scheduling strategy in modern LLM serving stacks (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, Orca) for online, latency-sensitive serving.

questions.prompt: What's the core limitation of static (request-level) batching?
options: It cannot run on GPUs with less than 80GB of memory
The whole batch can't be refreshed with new requests until every sequence in it finishes, wasting GPU cycles on padding
It requires every request to use the exact same prompt
It only works with models under 7B parameters
questions.explanation: Static batching ties the batch's lifetime to its slowest member: short sequences finish and then pad uselessly while new requests wait at the door, even when there's free GPU capacity to serve them.

questions.prompt: What does continuous batching change about WHEN the scheduler can admit or evict a request?
options: It admits and evicts requests at every decoding step, not just at batch boundaries
It only admits new requests once per minute regardless of GPU load
It evicts a request only after it has generated at least 1000 tokens
It batches requests across different GPUs but never within one GPU
questions.explanation: Orca's 'iteration-level scheduling' treats a single forward pass as the scheduling unit — finished sequences leave and new ones join on the very next step, keeping the batch continuously full.

questions.prompt: Why is continuous batching almost always paired with a paged (non-contiguous) KV cache?
options: Paged caches are a GPU vendor requirement
Sequences enter and leave the batch at arbitrary steps, so the cache can't assume one fixed, contiguous block shared by the whole batch
It reduces the model's total parameter count
It removes the need for a KV cache entirely
questions.explanation: Since batch membership changes every step, the memory manager has to allocate and free KV-cache space per sequence on the fly — exactly the problem a paged, block-based KV cache is built to solve.

posts.title: RetroChimera: Two Models That Disagree on Purpose
posts.subtitle: A transformer and a graph network vote on how to build a molecule — their disagreement is the signal.
posts.summary: Microsoft Research's RetroChimera ensembles a transformer and a graph neural network with opposite failure modes, then learns which to trust at each step. In blind expert tests it solved 9 of 10 hard synthesis targets and got roughly 90% of its routes accepted by chemists — more than double any single component or baseline.

slides.title: Planning Chemistry Backwards
slides.body: Synthesizing a new drug molecule means working backward from the target to ingredients you can actually buy — and most AI planners guess wrong in ways chemists spot immediately.

slides.title: Retrosynthesis Has a Combinatorial Explosion Problem
bullets: At every step, dozens of chemically valid 'disconnections' exist — picking the wrong one early can invalidate the whole route.
Three failure modes plague existing AI planners: missing rare-but-crucial reactions, breaking down on molecules unlike the training data, and proposing routes real chemists wouldn't recognize.
Synthesis planning is a major cost driver in drug development — a bad route wastes weeks of lab time before anyone notices.

slides.title: Two Models With Opposite Blind Spots, Plus a Referee
slides.body: RetroChimera doesn't pick one architecture — it runs two and learns when to trust each.
bullets: R-SMILES 2: a transformer that generates precursor molecules freely — flexible, but prone to hallucinating invalid chemistry.
NeuralLoc: a graph neural network that matches the target against a library of known reaction templates — reliable, but blind to reactions outside that library.
A learned re-ranker scores every candidate from both models, and votes add up when they agree — turning disagreement itself into a confidence signal.

slides.title: The Ensemble Beats Either Half by a Wide Margin
slides.body: On ten challenging targets, judged blind by PhD chemists:
bullets: In single-step blind tests, chemists rated RetroChimera's disconnections above both sub-models — and even above the literature reactions used as ground truth.

slides.title: Worked Example: Routing a Hard Target
slides.body: A chemist needs a synthesis route for a complex drug candidate with no obvious textbook pathway.
bullets: R-SMILES 2 proposes a creative but risky disconnection unlike anything literally seen in training data.
NeuralLoc independently proposes a different, template-backed disconnection that's lower-risk but more conventional.

Both models agree on the first retro-step but diverge afterward — the re-ranker boosts the agreed step and lets each model's independent middle-game play out, producing a full route experts accepted roughly 9 times in 10 on this class of target.

slides.title: Where RetroChimera Still Breaks
bullets: One wrong step invalidates an entire route — so even a 90% per-route acceptance rate means roughly 1 in 10 routes needs rework before it reaches the bench.
R-SMILES 2's free generation can still hallucinate chemically invalid structures; NeuralLoc simply can't propose anything outside its template library.
The headline numbers come from a 10-target expert evaluation — notable, but small next to the reaction counts in standard large-scale benchmarks.
Only two deep-learning sources were ensembled here; the authors note reaction databases and human-in-the-loop input are compatible but untested.

slides.title: Why This Pattern Travels Beyond Chemistry
bullets: Ensembling models with genuinely different failure modes — not just different random seeds — turns disagreement into a built-in confidence signal.
Published in Nature and open-sourced (weights + code on GitHub, plus access via Microsoft Foundry) by Microsoft Research AI for Science, September 2026.

The same 'two biased models + learned referee' recipe shows up anywhere a flexible generator and a constrained-but-reliable retriever trade off — not unlike RAG pipelines that blend dense and keyword search.

questions.prompt: What is RetroChimera's core architectural idea?
options: A single large transformer fine-tuned on reaction data
An ensemble of a free-form transformer and a template-based graph neural network, combined by a learned re-ranker
A reinforcement learning agent that searches reactions by trial and error
A retrieval system that only looks up past reactions

A single incorrect disconnection anywhere in the route invalidates the entire synthesis plan
Routes are graded independently of their steps
Chemists only check the final product, never the intermediate steps

options: It only works on molecules already in its training set
The expert evaluation covered just 10 challenging targets — a small sample next to standard large-scale benchmarks
It cannot be used for drug discovery at all
It requires a supercomputer to run inference

posts.title: Agent Memory: A Past Beyond the Context Window
posts.subtitle: A context window is a scratchpad, not a memory — here's how agents fake a durable one.
posts.summary: Every LLM call starts blank except for what fits in the prompt — fine for a one-off chatbot, a wall for an agent meant to remember you across weeks. MemGPT and Generative Agents solve this with two different mechanisms: OS-style memory paging, and periodic reflection. Here's how each actually works, and where both still fall apart.

slides.title: The Context Window Is Not a Memory
slides.body: Every LLM call starts blank except for what fits in the prompt. For a chatbot that's fine. For an agent that's supposed to remember you across weeks, it's a wall.

slides.title: Long-Running Agents Hit Two Walls at Once
bullets: Context windows are finite — stuff enough conversation history in and older turns get truncated or silently dropped.

Even within the window, LLMs don't weight all tokens equally — information buried in the middle of a long context is recalled less reliably than information near the start or end ('lost in the middle').
A session-only agent forgets everything the moment the window fills or the session ends — no persistent preferences, no accumulated world state.

slides.title: MemGPT's Fix: Treat the Context Window Like RAM
slides.body: MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023) borrows a decades-old OS idea — virtual memory — and applies it to LLMs.
bullets: Main context = fast 'RAM': a fixed block holding system instructions, working context, and a FIFO queue of recent messages — the only thing the LLM actually reads.
Archival + recall storage = slow 'disk': unbounded external storage the agent searches by issuing its own function calls, pulling results back into main context on demand.
An interrupt mechanism — MemGPT's analogue of a page fault — lets the model pause, evict older content, fetch what it actually needs, and resume instead of just losing it.

slides.title: A Second Approach: Reflect Instead of Just Store
slides.body: Generative Agents (Park et al., 2023) tackled the same problem from a different angle: don't just archive raw events — periodically synthesize them.
bullets: Every observation is logged as a natural-language memory with a timestamp and an importance score.
Periodically, the agent prompts itself to generate 'reflections' — higher-level insights synthesized from clusters of recent memories.
At decision time, memories are retrieved by a blend of recency, importance, and relevance to the current situation — not similarity search alone.

slides.title: Two Memory Strategies, Two Different Tradeoffs
bullets: Most production agent frameworks today mix both: a vector store for recall, plus periodic summarization to keep stored data from growing unbounded.

rows: Raw events + summaries, paged like OS memory

slides.title: Worked Example: A Coding Agent Across Three Sessions
slides.body: Session 1: you tell the agent your project uses pytest, not unittest. Session 3, two weeks later, you ask it to add a test.
bullets: Without memory: the agent has no idea what test framework you use — it guesses, often wrong, and rewrites boilerplate you already rejected.
With tiered memory: the preference was written to archival storage as a tagged fact; the agent issues a recall query ('testing conventions for this project') before writing code.

With reflection-style memory: enough small interactions accumulate into a synthesized note like 'user strongly prefers pytest fixtures over setUp/tearDown' — a generalization no single raw event stated outright.

slides.title: Where Agent Memory Breaks Down
bullets: Retrieval failure is silent — if the recall query misses the relevant memory, the agent confidently acts on nothing, and you often can't tell it forgot.
Unbounded memory growth means retrieval quality degrades over time unless old or redundant memories are pruned, decayed, or merged.
Reflection-style synthesis can calcify stale conclusions — an early reflection can bias retrieval long after preferences changed.
Memory read/write adds latency and cost (extra LLM calls or vector searches) — for short-lived, one-off tasks, it's pure overhead with no payoff.

slides.title: When to Reach for Each Pattern
bullets: Need precise, auditable recall of specific facts or documents → tiered/paged memory (MemGPT-style) with explicit search.
Need an agent whose judgment stays coherent over long horizons → reflection-style synthesis layered on raw logs.
Building a short, single-session tool-use agent → skip agent memory entirely; the context window is already enough.
Either way, memory is a retrieval problem wearing a different hat — the same recall/precision tradeoffs from RAG apply here too.

questions.prompt: What problem does agent memory solve that a bigger context window alone doesn't?
options: It makes the model generate faster
It gives the agent information that persists across sessions and survives when the window fills up, not just more room in one window
It eliminates the need for any retrieval
It makes token costs disappear
questions.explanation: Even a huge context window resets at the start of each session and still has a limit. Memory systems add persistence across sessions and selective recall of what's relevant — things raw window size doesn't provide on its own.

questions.prompt: In MemGPT's design, what plays the role of a page fault from OS virtual memory?
options: The system prompt
An interrupt that lets the model pause, evict old content from main context, and pull in needed data from archival/recall storage
A hardware exception
A network timeout
questions.explanation: MemGPT borrows OS virtual memory directly: main context is the limited 'RAM,' archival/recall storage is the 'disk,' and an interrupt — analogous to a page fault — lets the model page content in and out as needed.

questions.prompt: What's a real failure mode of reflection-based memory (Generative Agents style)?
options: It cannot store any information at all
Early reflections can become stale and keep biasing the agent's behavior even after the underlying facts have changed
It only works for coding agents
It requires no LLM calls to function
questions.explanation: Because reflections are synthesized conclusions, not raw facts, an outdated reflection can keep steering retrieval and behavior long after the situation that produced it changed — a form of staleness distinct from simple forgetting.

bullets: Context resets between the chat tool, the coding tool, and the automation tool
Long-running jobs die when the session or device disconnects
No single identity or audit trail when an agent touches sensitive systems

bullets: Four memory types: session, semantic, procedural, episodic

Every action logs to an audit trail attributed to that agent

Per-project spend caps auto-pause an agent; work resumes from the console

slides.body: You hand the coworker agent 200 vendor contracts before leaving the office. It keeps working after you close your laptop, flags risky clauses, and drops a summary in Drive by morning — no re-prompting required.

Ad hoc access to enterprise systems

posts.title: Semantic Caching: Skip the LLM, Reuse the Answer
posts.subtitle: Why answer a question the model has already answered, just worded differently?
posts.summary: Semantic caching stores past (query embedding, response) pairs and serves a cached answer whenever a new query is similar enough in embedding space — not just byte-for-byte identical. It can cut LLM calls and latency dramatically for FAQ-style traffic, but a loose similarity threshold or missing invalidation policy can just as easily serve a confident wrong answer.

slides.title: Most 'different' questions aren't actually different
slides.body: A support bot gets 'how do I reset my password' phrased fifty ways. An exact-match cache misses all of them; a semantic cache catches most.

slides.title: Paying full LLM price for the same question, every time
slides.body: Exact-match caching only helps when the input string is identical. Rephrasings, typos, and reorderings all miss the cache and trigger a fresh, costly model call.
bullets: A 10,000-query/day FAQ bot can have 30-40% of traffic be near-duplicates of earlier questions
Every missed cache hit means a full round-trip: tokenize, run the model, pay per-token
Latency for a cache miss is often 10-40x slower than a cache hit

slides.title: Match by meaning, not by bytes
slides.body: Embed the incoming query, search a vector store of (past query embedding → stored response) pairs, and if the closest match clears a similarity threshold, return the stored response without calling the LLM at all.
bullets: Different from exact-match caching: a hash/string lookup that only fires on identical input
Different from prompt/KV caching: that speeds up one model call by reusing a repeated prefix, it still calls the model
Semantic caching can skip the model call entirely for a repeat question

slides.title: Three moving parts, one tuning knob
slides.body: A small embedding model turns the query into a vector; a vector store (Redis, pgvector, Milvus) holds past query→response pairs; a similarity threshold decides what counts as 'close enough.'
bullets: Embedding step adds latency of its own — must stay far cheaper than the LLM call it's replacing
Threshold is usually cosine similarity, commonly tuned somewhere around 0.90-0.95
A TTL or invalidation hook is required wherever the underlying facts can change

slides.title: Worked example: a policy FAQ bot
slides.body: 'How many vacation days do I get?' and 'What's my PTO allowance?' embed close together. At a 0.93 cosine threshold, the second query hits the cache from the first — a 20ms vector lookup instead of an 800ms model call.
bullets: Cache hit: ~20ms (vector lookup only)
Cache miss: ~800ms (full LLM round-trip)
At 35% hit rate on 10,000 daily queries, that's roughly 3,500 LLM calls avoided per day

slides.title: Three caching layers, three different jobs

rows: Repeat of literally the same request
An entire model call for a reworded question

slides.title: When a loose threshold becomes a confident wrong answer
slides.body: 'Cancel my subscription' and 'cancel my order' can embed uncomfortably close. Set the threshold too loose and the cache returns a fluent, wrong answer with no indication anything went wrong.
bullets: Never cache personalized or real-time queries (account balance, order status) without scoping by user/session — or skip caching them entirely
Stale answers persist silently after a fact changes (pricing, policy) unless a TTL or invalidation hook exists
Below a certain query volume, embedding + vector-store overhead can cost more than it saves

slides.title: Cache the question, not just the string
bullets: Semantic caching trades an LLM call for an embedding lookup when two questions mean the same thing
It layers on top of, not instead of, exact-match and prompt/KV caching
The threshold is the whole system: too tight wastes cache hits, too loose serves wrong answers
Never cache anything personalized or time-sensitive without scoping or a TTL

questions.prompt: What's the key difference between semantic caching and exact-match caching?
options: Semantic caching is always faster to look up
Semantic caching matches by embedding similarity, so differently-worded repeats can still hit the cache
Exact-match caching uses a vector database
There is no real difference
questions.explanation: Exact-match caching only fires on an identical input string. Semantic caching embeds the query and matches by similarity, so 'reset my password' and 'how do I change my password' can both hit the same cached entry.

questions.prompt: What's a realistic failure mode of setting the similarity threshold too loose?
options: The cache never gets any hits
The LLM call becomes slower
Two different questions that embed close together (e.g. 'cancel my subscription' vs 'cancel my order') return the wrong cached answer
The embedding model crashes
questions.explanation: A loose threshold treats merely-similar queries as the-same-question, so the cache can confidently return an answer to a different question than the one actually asked.

questions.prompt: Why shouldn't you semantically cache a query like 'what's my current account balance'?
options: Because balance queries never repeat
Because the answer is personalized and time-sensitive, so a cached hit would likely serve someone else's or stale data
Because embeddings can't represent numbers
Because it would be too fast
questions.explanation: Semantic caching is built for questions whose correct answer is stable and shared across askers. A balance query's correct answer changes per-user and per-moment, so caching it without strict per-user scoping (or skipping it entirely) risks leaking or serving wrong data.

posts.title: Mixture of Experts: Scale Up Without Slowing Down
posts.subtitle: Give each token only a few experts to think with, not the whole model.
posts.summary: Mixture of Experts replaces a dense feed-forward block with many smaller expert blocks plus a learned router that activates only a handful per token. This decouples total model capacity from per-token compute cost, letting models scale to huge parameter counts cheaply — at the price of harder training and heavier memory/communication demands at serving time.

slides.title: The Trick Behind Trillion-Parameter Models
slides.body: Mixture of Experts (MoE) lets a model have enormous total capacity while only 'thinking' with a small slice of it on any given token.

slides.title: Dense Models Pay for Every Parameter, Every Token
slides.body: A dense transformer's feed-forward layers activate 100% of their weights for every single token, no matter how simple that token is.
bullets: Dense feed-forward blocks run the full matrix multiply for every token — there's no 'this token doesn't need all this math' shortcut.
Compute per token scales directly with total parameters: roughly double the params, roughly double the FLOPs per token.
Labs wanted trillion-parameter capacity without a trillion-parameter inference bill.

slides.title: Route Each Token to a Few Specialist Experts
slides.body: MoE swaps the single dense FFN for many smaller 'expert' FFNs plus a tiny gating network that picks which experts handle each token.
bullets: A router — a small learned layer — scores every expert for a token and selects only the top-k highest scoring ones (commonly k=1 or k=2).
Only the selected experts run their FFN on that token; every unselected expert contributes zero compute for it.
Total parameters across all experts can be huge, while the active compute per token stays small.

slides.title: The Hard Part Is Keeping Experts Balanced
slides.body: The routing math is simple; the engineering problem is making sure every expert actually gets trained and used.
bullets: Switch Transformer (Google, 2021) used top-1 routing — just 1 of N experts per token — to scale past a trillion parameters while keeping per-token compute comparable to a far smaller dense model.
Each expert has a capacity (max tokens it can accept per batch); tokens that overflow get dropped or sent to a fallback — a real quality tradeoff, not a free lunch.
An auxiliary load-balancing loss penalizes the router whenever it funnels too many tokens to the same few experts, preventing 'expert collapse.'

slides.title: Same Compute, Very Different Capacity
slides.body: Mixtral 8x7B makes the tradeoff concrete: most of its parameters sit idle on any given token.

slides.title: Watch a Router Specialize — Without Being Told To
slides.body: Picture an MoE model processing: "The patient's white blood cell count was elevated."
bullets: The router may learn to send tokens like 'patient' and 'blood' toward experts that, through gradient descent alone, drifted toward medical vocabulary.
Feed the same model "The hedge fund's short position was elevated" and 'hedge' and 'position' can land on entirely different experts — no human labeled any of this.
Caveat: real routing is usually messier than clean topic specialization — it often splits more by syntax or token frequency — but the mechanism is identical either way.

slides.title: The Bill Comes Due in Memory and Infrastructure
slides.body: MoE trades compute for complexity — and that complexity shows up in serving memory and training infrastructure, not model quality.
bullets: Memory doesn't shrink: every expert must stay resident across your GPUs even though a token only touches a couple — Mixtral still has to hold all 8 experts, not just the 2 it uses.
Distributed training needs all-to-all GPU communication to ship each token to the right expert's device — a genuine network bottleneck at scale (expert parallelism).
Fine-tuning is twitchy: a learning-rate or data shift can trigger router collapse, where most tokens pile onto 1-2 experts and the rest go stale.
Skip MoE for small models or single-GPU serving — there's no spare memory budget or distributed infrastructure to amortize the routing overhead against.

slides.title: Capacity and Compute, Decoupled
bullets: MoE decouples total parameters from per-token compute: huge capacity, small active compute per token.
A router picks the top-k experts per token; everything hinges on an auxiliary loss keeping that routing balanced.
The price isn't accuracy — it's engineering: all experts must fit in distributed memory, and tokens must be shuttled to the right device.
Reach for MoE when raw capacity matters more than serving simplicity; skip it when you can't amortize the memory and communication overhead.

questions.prompt: In an MoE layer with top-2 routing out of 8 experts, how many experts actually process a given token?
options: All 8
Only 2
Only 1
A random number each time
questions.explanation: Top-k routing with k=2 means the gate scores all 8 experts and sends the token only to the 2 highest-scoring ones — the other 6 do zero work for that token. That's exactly where MoE's compute savings come from.

questions.prompt: Why do MoE models need an auxiliary 'load-balancing' loss during training?
options: To make the model's output more creative
To stop the router from sending most tokens to just one or two favorite experts, leaving the rest undertrained
To reduce the total number of parameters
To speed up tokenization
questions.explanation: Without a balancing signal, gradient descent tends to funnel tokens to whichever experts got a head start — a feedback loop called router/expert collapse. The auxiliary loss penalizes imbalance so every expert gets trained and used.

questions.prompt: A Mixtral-style MoE model has far more total parameters than a same-active-compute dense model. What's the main operational cost of that extra capacity?
options: Slower token generation because every expert runs on every token
Higher memory requirements, since all experts must stay resident even though only a few are used per token
It can no longer be fine-tuned
It always produces lower-quality output
questions.explanation: MoE saves compute, not memory — every expert's weights must sit in GPU memory (or be reachable across a cluster) even though a given token only activates a couple of them. That's why MoE serving is memory- and communication-heavy, not compute-heavy.

posts.title: The Missing Map of the Sky: Claude Fills GALEX's Gaps
posts.subtitle: A swarm of agents stitched a decade-old UV survey gap into one self-correcting map
posts.summary: Astrophysicist Brice Ménard used Claude Science to stitch NASA's GALEX ultraviolet survey (which deliberately skipped a third of the sky to protect its detectors) with other missions, then trained an inpainting model to fill the gap with per-pixel confidence estimates. Claude's agents also caught and fixed their own calibration mistake across 38,000 observations.

slides.title: A Third of the UV Sky Had No Data — For Over a Decade
slides.body: NASA's GALEX mission mapped about two-thirds of the sky in ultraviolet between 2003 and 2013. The rest sat blank, flagged as too risky to shoot.
bullets: GALEX ran 38,000 separate observations between 2003-2013
It deliberately skipped the Milky Way's plane and regions near bright stars
Filling the gap by hand needed weeks of pixel-level calibration — so it never got done

slides.title: Why Nobody Finished the Job
slides.body: Ultraviolet light is absorbed by Earth's atmosphere, so it can only be observed from space — and space telescopes have fragile detectors.
bullets: Bright stars can saturate or damage a UV detector, so GALEX's team programmed it to avoid them entirely
Other missions (Swift, South Korea's FIMS/SPEAR, Europe's TD-1) covered scraps of the gap, but in different resolutions and calibrations
Merging incompatible instruments onto one coordinate grid is exactly the kind of tedious, error-prone work that stays a backlog item forever

slides.title: Claude Science Ran the Pipeline as a Swarm of Agents
slides.body: Ménard gave high-level direction; many Claude agents executed the pipeline in parallel.
bullets: Collect: agents found and downloaded tens of thousands of public GALEX images plus Swift and FIMS/SPEAR data
Clean: agents removed stellar glare around bright stars so faint UV signal underneath could be measured
Merge: cross-calibrated every instrument, resampled to one resolution, and placed them on a shared coordinate system
Fill: trained an inpainting model on the relationship between UV and the visible/infrared/radio data available everywhere, then applied it to the unobserved third with per-pixel confidence scores

slides.title: When the Map Was Wrong, Claude Found Its Own Mistake
slides.body: Validation wasn't just a final check — it caught a real error mid-pipeline.
bullets: To validate, Claude hid patches of known UV data, predicted them blind, and compared — after several refinement rounds, predictions landed within about 10% of real measurements
But circular artifacts from residual atmospheric glow in individual GALEX pointings slipped past two full rounds of automated agent review
Once Ménard flagged the pattern, Claude re-processed and corrected all 38,000 observations in a few hours

slides.title: Where This Map Should Make You Cautious
slides.body: A map that's one-third inferred is genuinely useful — but only if you remember which third.
bullets: About a third of the final map, including much of the galactic plane, is predicted by the model, not directly observed by any telescope
Inpainting assumes UV brightness correlates with visible/infrared/radio data — it will quietly fail on any genuinely novel UV source that breaks that correlation
Two rounds of autonomous agent review missed the glow artifacts; it took a human scientist's eye to catch the pattern — autonomous validation isn't foolproof yet

slides.title: What Each Data Source Contributed
Why This Matters
slides.body: This isn't a toy demo — it's a public scientific resource with its uncertainty labeled.
bullets: Every pixel in the final map is tagged 'measured' or 'predicted,' with an uncertainty estimate attached
The map adds UV brightness estimates for more than 100 million individual stars, inferred from Gaia's visible-light data
It's public at menard.pha.jhu.edu/uvmap, covering far-UV (154nm) and near-UV (232nm), and shows real structures: dust clouds, supernova gas-bubble rings, and the Magellanic Clouds
The workflow — a scientist directs, agents execute and iterate, a human catches the one systematic error agents missed — is the template, not the astronomy itself

options: Funding ran out before the mission finished
To protect its detectors from bright stars
Those regions already had complete UV data from other missions
Cloud cover on Earth blocked those observations
questions.explanation: GALEX's detectors could be saturated or damaged by intense UV light, so the mission was programmed to avoid bright-star regions and the Milky Way's plane entirely.

options: It compared results to a panel of astronomers' rankings

posts.title: Claude Code Review Goes GA: 3x Faster, Three Depth Settings
posts.subtitle: Automatic review on every pull request, tunable from Quick to Deep
posts.summary: Claude Code Review exited research preview on October 15, 2026, and is now on by default for Claude Team and Enterprise organizations. Reviews run about 3x faster than in preview (6-10 minutes versus ~20), admins can tune depth per repository, and developers get automatic reviews on new PRs with zero configuration.

slides.title: Code Review Ships to Every Pull Request — Automatically
slides.body: What was a research preview is now a standing part of the PR workflow for Claude Team and Enterprise orgs.
bullets: Exited research preview on October 15, 2026
Triggers automatically on every new pull request once enabled — zero configuration for developers
Anthropic runs it on its own pull requests before shipping features

slides.title: Preview Was Accurate But Too Slow to Trust in CI
slides.body: A 20-minute review can't realistically gate a merge — by the time it finishes, the team has already moved on.
bullets: Original preview reviews took roughly 20 minutes per PR
Teams wanted reviews fast enough to actually block a merge, not just arrive as a slow, advisory afterthought
Too many low-value comments bury the one bug that actually matters

slides.title: Three Knobs: Quick, Standard, Deep
slides.body: Instead of one fixed review mode, admins choose depth per repository.
bullets: Quick — fastest, cheapest pass, for lower-stakes repos
Standard — the default, balances speed and thoroughness
Deep — full architectural review for high-stakes repos, trading speed for scrutiny
Setup is entirely admin-side: install the GitHub App, enable Code Review, pick a depth per repo — developers change nothing

slides.title: What Actually Changed Under the Hood
slides.body: The speedup wasn't just infrastructure — the review format itself got tighter.
bullets: Reviews now typically finish in about 6-10 minutes, down from roughly 20 — close to a 3x speedup
Findings are now structured as problem, trigger condition, and fix — cutting the noise of low-value comments
Anthropic dogfoods Code Review on its own pull requests as part of validating each change

slides.title: Same PR, Three Different Depths
slides.body: The depth setting changes what kind of review a given pull request gets, not just how long it takes.
bullets: Quick depth on a small docs-only PR: a fast pass that flags only clear, obvious issues
Standard depth on a typical feature PR: catches logic bugs and edge cases within the normal 6-10 minute window
Deep depth on a PR touching auth or billing code: slower, broader architectural scrutiny — reserved deliberately for high-stakes changes, not run by default everywhere

posts.title: Consistent Hashing: Scaling Without a Full Reshuffle
posts.subtitle: Why adding one node shouldn't move 80% of your keys
posts.summary: Plain hash(key) % N remaps most keys every time a node joins or leaves a cluster. Consistent hashing fixes this by placing nodes and keys on the same ring so only a local neighborhood of keys moves — and virtual nodes keep that movement evenly spread across the real machines.

slides.title: Add One More Node Without Reshuffling Everything
slides.body: Consistent hashing is the technique behind scaling caches and databases without a cache-miss storm every time the cluster changes size.
bullets: Naive hash(key) % N remaps almost every key when N changes
Consistent hashing keeps roughly 1/N of keys moving when a node joins or leaves
Used in DynamoDB, Cassandra, memcached clients, CDNs, and load balancers

slides.title: Why hash(key) % N Breaks at Scale
slides.body: The modulo operation ties every key's owner directly to the total node count — so the moment that count changes, almost nothing stays put.
bullets: Changing N from 4 to 5 nodes relocates roughly (N-1)/N of all keys — about 80% churn
Every node addition or removal triggers a mass cache-miss storm across the whole cluster
At scale, with hundreds of shards, this makes routine horizontal scaling operationally painful

slides.title: Put Nodes and Keys on the Same Ring
slides.body: Instead of hashing keys against a count, hash both nodes and keys onto one fixed circular space.
bullets: Hash both server IDs and keys onto a fixed ring, e.g. the range 0 to 2^32-1
A key belongs to the first node found clockwise from its position on the ring
Adding a node only steals keys from its immediate clockwise neighbor — not from every other node in the cluster

slides.title: Virtual Nodes Fix the Lumpy-Ring Problem
slides.body: A handful of physical nodes placed directly on the ring creates uneven arcs — some nodes end up owning far more keys than others.
bullets: Fix: hash each physical node into 100-200 virtual points scattered around the ring, instead of just one
Load evens out because the uneven-arc variance averages away across many virtual positions per real node
This is exactly what Cassandra and DynamoDB both do in production to keep load balanced

slides.title: Worked Example: 4 Nodes Become 5
slides.body: A ring holding nodes A, B, C, D at fixed hash positions, with keys assigned clockwise.
bullets: Adding node E inserts it onto the ring between C and D
Only the keys that previously mapped to D and fall before E's new position move to E — roughly 1/5 of total keys
Every other node's keys (A, B, C, and D's remaining keys) are completely untouched by the change

slides.title: Key Movement: Mod-N vs. Consistent Hashing

rows: No — only the new node's ring neighbor

slides.title: When It's Overkill or Risky
slides.body: Consistent hashing solves a real problem, but it's not free complexity you want everywhere.
bullets: For a fixed, rarely-resized cluster, plain mod-N hashing is simpler and perfectly fine — don't add ring complexity you don't need
Without virtual nodes, a small number of physical nodes can still land unevenly on the ring and get a lumpy load distribution
Consistent hashing alone doesn't handle replication — systems like DynamoDB add a replication factor on top, storing each key on the next R nodes clockwise

slides.title: Why This Matters
slides.body: The core idea generalizes far beyond caches — it's the same trick behind sharding and request routing at scale.
bullets: Core idea: map nodes and keys onto the same ring so only a local neighborhood of keys moves when membership changes
Virtual nodes are what actually make load balanced in real production systems — not the ring alone
In use today in DynamoDB, Cassandra, Riak, and many CDN and load-balancer designs
Interview tip: always mention virtual nodes — that's almost always the follow-up question after you describe the basic ring

questions.prompt: With plain hash(key) % N, what happens when a cluster goes from 4 nodes to 5?
options: No keys move
About 20% of keys move
About 80% of keys move
Exactly one key moves
questions.explanation: Mod-N hashing ties every key's owner to the total node count N, so changing N remaps roughly (N-1)/N of all keys — about 80% churn going from 4 to 5 nodes.

questions.prompt: What problem do 'virtual nodes' solve in a consistent hashing scheme?
options: They encrypt data on the ring
They replace the need for a hash function
They even out load when a small number of physical nodes land unevenly on the ring
They eliminate the need for a hash ring entirely
questions.explanation: A few physical nodes placed directly on the ring can create uneven arcs. Hashing each physical node into 100-200 virtual positions averages that variance away, balancing load across real machines.

questions.prompt: When node E is inserted onto the ring between nodes C and D, which keys move to E?
options: Every key in the system
Only the keys that previously belonged to D and now fall before E's position
A random 50% sample of all keys
No keys move — only metadata changes
questions.explanation: Only the keys in the arc between C and E's new position — previously owned by D — move to E. Every other node's keys are untouched, which is the whole point of consistent hashing.

posts.title: OpenGCUA: Letting the Model Run Your Whole Computer
posts.subtitle: Code execution plus harness-to-model decision transfer cuts agent steps 53%
posts.summary: OpenGCUA, an open stack from Alibaba's Tongyi-MAI team, lets agents write code instead of clicking one GUI element at a time, and moves key decisions from a fixed harness into the model itself. Across eight frontier models on OSWorld-v2, mean partial score rose from 45.3 to 64.9 while steps per task fell 53%.

slides.title: Why Can't an Agent Just Use a Whole Computer?
slides.body: Frontier computer-use agents like GPT-6 Astra are closed systems. A new open stack, OpenGCUA, tries to show what makes them work — and open-sources the whole pipeline.

slides.title: GUI-Only Agents Hardcode Three Decisions
slides.body: Most computer-use agents fix the same three choices inside the harness, not the model.
bullets: What to observe: take a fresh screenshot after every single action, even trivial ones
How to act: one GUI click, type, or scroll per step — no branching, no loops
How to track progress: no persistent plan across a long task

slides.title: Two Ideas: Code Execution + Decision Transfer
slides.body: OpenGCUA's core move is handing those three decisions to the model instead of the scaffold.
bullets: Code execution: the model writes a Python program per step that mixes accessibility-tree reads, app APIs, shell commands, and GUI clicks — with loops and branches
Harness-to-model decision transfer: the model decides when it actually needs a screenshot, instead of taking one every step
Before each program it writes an <intent> statement and keeps a running todo list, so planning survives across dozens of steps

slides.title: The Numbers: Fewer Steps, Higher Scores
slides.body: Measured on the OSWorld-v2 offline benchmark across eight frontier models (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5, Gemini 3.8 Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash, Qwen3.8-Max, Qwen3.8-Flash, Kimi K3, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash).

slides.title: Worked Example: Reorganizing 200 Files
slides.body: Imagine the task is 'sort these 200 downloaded files into folders by date modified.'
bullets: GUI-only agent: screenshot, click file, read date, drag to folder, screenshot again — repeated 200 times, burning hundreds of steps
OpenGCUA agent: writes one short script that reads all file metadata via the accessibility API and loops to move each file, taking a screenshot only to confirm the result
The paper reports code execution alone adds +6.1 points and cuts steps 14.8% versus GUI+CLI access, averaged over three models

slides.title: Weaker Models Gain the Most — and Limits Remain
slides.body: The gains aren't evenly spread, and the real-device story is still early.
bullets: GLM-5.3-Flash improved +35.2 points and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash +29.8 — code execution narrows the gap between strong and weak models more than it widens it
On four real macOS tasks, Qwen3.8-Max burned 19.4x the reasoning tokens of GPT-6 Astra and still finished only 3 of 4 tasks, versus 4 of 4 for GPT-6 Astra
The real-device harness and cross-device SDK are both marked 'preliminary' — this is a research preview, not a production agent

slides.title: Why This Matters
slides.body: OpenGCUA is a case for an architectural idea, not just a leaderboard entry.
bullets: Letting models write code to interact with a computer, instead of clicking through a fixed GUI loop, is a more general interface than screenshot-and-click
Full trajectories for all eight evaluated models are public, so anyone can study why one model times out or loops where another doesn't
Released under Apache-2.0 with code, prompts, and eval trajectories — a rare fully-open look at a computer-use stack

options: A bigger model and more training data
Code execution and harness-to-model decision transfer

Reinforcement learning from human feedback on clicks
questions.explanation: OpenGCUA's headline contribution is letting the model write code to act (instead of one GUI click per step) and moving decisions like 'when to look at the screen' from the fixed harness into the model.

questions.explanation: Across eight frontier models, mean partial score rose from 45.3 to 64.9 while steps per task dropped 53% on average — fewer, more effective actions per task.

questions.prompt: Which models benefited most from the OpenGCUA approach?
options: The strongest models got relatively stronger, widening the gap
All models gained identically
Weaker models like GLM-5.3-Flash and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash gained the most, shrinking the gap between strongest and weakest
Only closed frontier models like GPT-6 Astra improved
questions.explanation: The strongest-to-weakest score gap shrank from 39.1 to 18.0 points, driven by large gains for weaker models — code execution seems to compensate for weaker raw reasoning.

posts.title: Scion: Why Anthropic Replaced Git in Its Own Monorepo
posts.subtitle: Always-online clients, a server that owns history, and ~200x less infrastructure
posts.summary: Anthropic migrated its entire monorepo off git to an in-house system called Scion, built around always-online clients and a server that owns history, blame, and merges. The result: about 200x less infrastructure than the old git mirror fleet and checkouts that take seconds instead of minutes.

slides.title: Why Anthropic Stopped Using Git
slides.body: Claude-written code grew Anthropic's monorepo faster than git's distributed, offline-first design could handle — so they built a replacement: Scion.

slides.title: Git Wasn't Built for an Always-Online Fleet of Agents
slides.body: Daily merged changes rose from about 2,500 in May 2026 to over 30,000 by September — roughly 12x in four months.
bullets: Main branch history is nearly 100GB; a compressed working copy alone is over 25GB
About 25 million checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer machines, agent sandboxes, and research jobs
A naive git fetch model at that volume implies over 600 petabytes of traffic a day
Several hundred internal git mirrors were running at peak just to keep up, and they kept drifting from the tip of main

slides.title: Scion: Assume the Client Is Always Online
slides.body: Instead of git's offline-first model where every clone holds the full history, Scion flips the assumption.
bullets: Clients fetch data on demand from a reachable server rather than syncing a full copy
The server owns history, blame, commits, merges, and rebases; the client just keeps a bounded local cache
'Source control as an API': CI jobs and bisect/revert tools can query history or run operations with no local repository at all
Commits happen server-side with no push step, so cost scales with the size of the change, not the size of the repo

slides.title: Three Tiers, One Protocol
slides.body: Scion's data model is a changeset in a write-ahead log, not a git-style tree snapshot.
bullets: A changeset lists only the files changed relative to its first parent, with content-addressed pointers to compressed blobs
scion-daemon runs per node for local jobs; scion-cache runs per region and streams objects from memory; scion-server is authoritative, backed by Spanner and cloud storage
Ref updates (like moving 'main') are a compare-and-swap on a single Spanner row, decoupled from changeset creation
Design borrows from Google's Piper and Meta's Sapling/Mononoke, whose Bonsai data model directly influenced Scion's changesets

slides.title: Git Mirror Fleet vs. Scion
Worked Example: A Bisect Job With No Checkout
slides.body: An automated bisect pipeline needs to find which of 10,000 commits introduced a regression.
bullets: On git, that means cloning or fetching enough history locally to walk the commit graph, then checking out candidate commits one by one
On Scion, the bisect tool calls the history API directly — reading ancestry and blame as RPCs — and only materializes a sparse working copy for the final candidate it needs to actually run
Anthropic also had Claude Mythos Preview rewrite the hand-built git-to-Scion ingestion pipeline itself, cutting its memory use 20x and roughly quadrupling its speed

slides.title: Not a General Git Replacement
slides.body: Anthropic is explicit that Scion only pays off at a specific kind of scale.
bullets: It only makes sense for enormous monorepos with heavy always-online CI and agent traffic — not a typical multi-repo team's workflow
Migrating took a dedicated team of seven people about five months, plus building a matching code review tool (Antique), code search, and a new IAM system alongside it
Global merge locks don't fit agent-scale commit rates, so Scion leans on post-merge and pre-deploy testing instead — occasional conflicts slip through and get fixed after the fact
Anthropic is still working with GitHub, GitLab, and the open-source community on whether any of these ideas (server-side RPCs, scalable server architectures) can go mainstream

slides.title: Why This Matters
slides.body: Scion is a concrete data point on what breaks when AI agents, not just humans, become your main committers.
bullets: Git's core assumption — every client eventually holds a full, offline copy of history — stops scaling once checkouts are driven by thousands of always-online CI jobs and agent sandboxes
Treating source control as a queryable API, not just a sync protocol, let Anthropic cut infrastructure roughly 200x versus its old mirror fleet
It's a preview of an infrastructure problem other large AI labs and engineering orgs will likely hit as agentic coding volume grows

questions.prompt: What's the central design shift Scion makes versus git?
options: Scion stores more data on each client than git does
Scion assumes clients are always online and fetch on demand, while the server owns history, blame, and merges
Scion removes the need for a server entirely
Scion only works for single-file repositories
questions.explanation: Git is distributed and offline-first: every clone eventually holds a full copy. Scion assumes clients are always connected, so they fetch what they need on demand while the server stays authoritative over history.

questions.prompt: What triggered Anthropic to build Scion in the first place?
options: A security vulnerability discovered in git
A licensing dispute with GitHub
Daily merged changes grew roughly 12x in four months, overwhelming git-based infrastructure
A decision to open-source all internal tooling
questions.explanation: Daily merged changes rose from about 2,500 in May 2026 to over 30,000 by September, driven largely by AI-assisted coding — git's offline-first design and the surrounding mirror fleet couldn't keep up.

questions.prompt: According to Anthropic, when does Scion's approach make sense?
options: For any team using git, regardless of size
Only for small personal projects
Only for enormous monorepos with heavy always-online CI and agent traffic — not a general git replacement
Only for repositories with no CI pipeline
questions.explanation: Anthropic is explicit that Scion isn't a general-purpose git replacement — it only pays off at a scale where hundreds of git mirrors and tens of millions of daily checkouts were already straining, and it requires building matching review, search, and CI tooling.
